evidence.excerpt:
Enqueue adds a new entry at the next open leaf position so the complete shape is preserved. All old parent-child relations are unchanged. Only the new entry's path toward the root can violate min-heap order. Bubble-up compares with the parent and swaps while the child is smaller. Moving upward strictly decreases its index, so repair terminates.

Start with [2, 5, 4] and enqueue 1. Appending produces [2, 5, 4, 1]. Comparing 1 with parent 5 gives [2, 1, 4, 5]. Comparing that 1 with root 2 gives [1, 2, 4, 5]. Do not sort the whole array; that would enforce a stronger and more expensive condition than the operation needs.

Dequeue first saves the root result. Move the last live entry to the root and reduce Count. The only possible ordering defects now lie downward from that replacement. Choose the smaller existing child before swapping; exchanging with an arbitrary child can leave a smaller sibling above a larger parent relation.

| Heap after removing 1 | Inspection | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [5, 2, 4] | Children 2 and 4 | Choose 2 |
| [2, 5, 4] | 5 has no child | Stop |

A singleton removal needs no child access after Count becomes zero. An empty removal must follow the stated failure policy without first reading position zero. Also clear unused reference slots when the implementation owns a backing array and should release references to removed objects. Reducing Count hides a slot from the abstract sequence, but it does not itself erase a stored reference.

The height of a complete heap is logarithmic in its live size, which bounds the number of repair levels. Array growth can add copying to an enqueue, so qualify an operation's cost rather than ignoring representation maintenance. evidence.excerpt:
The pattern `IEnumerable<T> Produce(...) { ... yield return value; ... }` defines an iterator. Yielding supplies one element and suspends that enumeration's progress until the consumer requests another. An ordinary return from a value-returning method finishes that call; yield return participates in a sequence of resumptions. Explain this distinction before treating yield as abbreviated list construction.

Laziness changes when work and failures occur. Obtaining an enumerable need not run every statement that will produce its values. If the consumer stops after two elements, later elements may never be computed. An expensive calculation inside an iterator is not paid simply because an enumerable variable has been declared, but repeated enumerations may repeat that work. Do not promise caching unless the implementation explicitly provides it.

The producer also needs a mutation policy. An enumeration over shared mutable storage can be affected by changes made after the enumerable is obtained. Library collections may detect invalid mutation during enumeration; custom types must state their own behavior. Returning IEnumerable<T> does not automatically create a snapshot or make private storage immutable.

Guided prediction: an iterator announces each produced number and yields 2, 4, 6. A caller breaks after consuming 4. Which production announcements should appear? Then run a second enumeration and ask whether it starts with a fresh progress state. Use the existing runnable iterator examples to check your prediction and distinguish fresh enumeration from continuing one enumerator.

Before choosing class, struct or record, ask what one value means, whether it can change, and what callers should expect when it is assigned or compared. Assigning a struct variable copies its value. That copy contains the values of its fields; if one of those fields is itself a reference, both copies can still refer to a shared object. Value-type copying is not a promise that every reachable object has been recursively duplicated. A record class is a reference type with compiler-supported value-oriented equality and copying syntax; assigning its variable still copies a reference. A record struct combines record features with value-type copying.

| Choice | Assignment behavior | Design question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ordinary class instance | Another reference to the same object | Is identity and a controlled lifecycle important? |
| Struct value | Copy of its fields | Is this a small coherent value with a meaningful default? |
| Record class instance | Another reference on assignment | Does value-oriented equality fit a reference-based data model? |
| Record struct value | Copy of its fields | Do both value copying and record conveniences fit? |

For positional records, the parameter list declares the data used by generated members. A with expression creates a copied result with selected changes; it is not a deep-cloning operator. If a copied record contains a mutable list, later changes to that list may be visible through both record objects. evidence.excerpt:
Sorting has at least two obligations: output order must satisfy the chosen comparison policy, and output must contain exactly the input occurrences. Producing 1, 2, 3 from input 3, 1, 2 looks right, but so would returning a fixed 1, 2, 3 regardless of input. Tests need to challenge preservation as well as ordering.

Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix. The next item is saved outside the moving region. Larger prefix items shift one position right until the saved item fits. Assigning the saved item back closes the hole. This explains why writing over the next item before saving it can lose data even though the remaining positions appear ordered.

| Input prefix and next item | Work | Resulting prefix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [4], next 2 | Save 2, shift 4, insert 2 | [2, 4] |
| [2, 4], next 3 | Save 3, shift 4, insert 3 | [2, 3, 4] |

Before each outer iteration, the processed prefix is sorted and is a permutation of the corresponding original prefix. The inner shifts preserve all saved occurrences while opening the correct position. When the prefix includes the full array, both obligations hold. This is a reasoning structure, not simply a description of what a successful example happened to print.

Equal keys reveal another contract. If the inner loop moves only items strictly greater than the saved key, equal-key items retain their previous relative order. This is stability. Moving equal items as well can change that order. Use labeled records, such as two invoices with the same total but different IDs, to see the distinction; identical integer values cannot show which occurrence moved.

For price 12 and quantity three, independently calculate 36 before running either version. A fixed packing charge of four makes the order total 40. Keep these two contracts distinct: LineTotal returns 36; OrderTotal returns 40. If the extracted line calculation starts adding packing as well, a caller that already adds packing can charge it twice even though both helper methods contain plausible arithmetic.

| Refactoring stage | Evidence to retain |
| --- | --- |
| Before extraction | Expected amount and current observable output |
| After extracting LineTotal | Same line amount for ordinary and zero inputs |
| After composing OrderTotal | Exactly one application of the fixed charge |
| After formatting a report | Same numerical meaning; display policy stays explicit |

A **statement** instructs the program to do something. In the example, statements execute in order from top to bottom. This is **sequential execution**. A later instruction does not change output already printed by an earlier one.

Other programming constructs select between actions or repeat them. Chapters 3 and 5 teach decisions and iteration. You do not need those constructs to write your first useful output program.

A **syntax error** violates the language's rules and can prevent compilation. A **logical error** occurs when instructions run but produce an unintended result. Printing an outdated appointment time may compile successfully while still misleading a customer. Compilation is one check, not proof that the program is correct. Chapter 6 develops debugging and testing.

evidence.excerpt:
All rows must be the same length when using this notation.

Often two dimensional arrays, like one dimensional arrays, are processed
in loops. Multiple dimension arrays are often processed in nested loops.
We could print out this table using columns 5 spaces wide with the code:

```csharp
         for (int r = 0; r < 3; r++) {
            for (int c = 0; c < 4; c++) {
               Console.Write("{0, 5}", table[r, c]);
            }
            Console.WriteLine();
         }
```

If we wanted to make a more general function out of that code,
we have a problem: the number of rows and columns were literal values
that we knew. We need something more general. For one dimensional
arrays we had the Length property, but now there are more than one
lengths!

The following standalone example illustrates the syntax needed:


int[, ] table = { {2, 4,  7, 55},
                  {3, 1,  8, 10},
                  {6, 0, 49, 12} };
Console.WriteLine(table.Length);        // get the total number of elements
Console.WriteLine(table.GetLength(0));  // get number of elements in the 1st dimension (rows)
Console.WriteLine(table.GetLength(1));  // get number of elements in the 2nd dimension (columns)
foreach (int n in table) {
   Console.Write($"{n} ");
}


Note:

- The meaning for the Length property,
  is now the *total* number of elements, (3)(4) = 12.
- The separate method `GetLength` is needed to find the number of rows and columns.
  The entries in the list of array indices in the multi-dimensional array notation
  are themselves indexed to provide the `GetLength` method parameter for each dimension.
  In this case index 0 gives the row length (left index of the array notation),
  and 1 gives the column length (right index of the array notation).
